lines.text: The temples of Angkor, a great empire, French rule and the terror of the Khmer Rouge. This is the story of Cambodia, and how it rebuilt.
It begins with the Mekong, flowing down from Tibet for millions of years, its fish and rice fields feeding the lands along it.
On the lower Mekong rose Funan, an early kingdom that grew rich on trade by sea.
In 802 a Khmer king founded an empire at Angkor. Its rulers built hundreds of temples and great reservoirs to water the rice.
Its greatest builder, Jayavarman the seventh, would raise the walled city of Angkor Thom and the smiling faces of the Bayon.
Around 1150 Angkor Wat was completed for King Suryavarman the second, the largest religious monument in the world. It is on the flag today.
In 1186 came Ta Prohm, a temple that giant tree roots now hold in their grip.
As Angkor declined, the Khmer moved south, and Phnom Penh grew on the river to become the capital.
Squeezed between its neighbours, Cambodia came under French protection in 1863, and France ruled for ninety years.
Norodom Sihanouk, born in 1922, would become king and lead the country to independence.
Pol Pot, born a few years later, would lead the Khmer Rouge to power and empty the cities.
Hun Sen, born in 1952, would later rule as prime minister for nearly forty years.
In 1953 Sihanouk won independence from France, and the Kingdom of Cambodia stood on its own again.
But war crept in from Vietnam, and the communist Khmer Rouge grew in the countryside. In 1975 they took Phnom Penh.
Over the next four years, through executions, forced labour and famine, well over a million Cambodians died.
In the capital, a school became the prison S-21, Tuol Sleng. About eighteen thousand people were held there, and very few survived.
In December 1978 Vietnam invaded and drove the Khmer Rouge from power, though fighting went on for years.
Hun Manet, the son of Hun Sen, was born in 1977. He would succeed his father as prime minister in 2023.
In 1991 the Paris Peace Agreements finally ended the long Cambodian war.
The United Nations stepped in to run the country for a time, and held free elections in 1993.
And a special court was set up to try the surviving Khmer Rouge leaders for genocide, decades after their crimes.
From the glory of Angkor through the darkest years, Cambodia has found its way back to peace.
